title: The AI Physician
answer: Ten areas where artificial intelligence is changing medicine: imaging, genomics, clinical documentation, surgery, intensive care, drug discovery, telemedicine, population health, the brain, and the regulation and security of the devices doing the work.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology
children.blurb: Detection and triage, synthetic imaging, 3D anatomical models, ultrasound enhancement and radiomics.

children.name: Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics
children.blurb: Polygenic risk, gene editing design, pharmacogenomics, epigenetic age and rare disease diagnosis.

children.name: Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence
children.blurb: Ambient scribes, coding, patient summaries, decision support and multilingual intake.

children.name: Surgical Robotics and Navigation
children.blurb: Resection planning, haptic feedback, virtual rehearsal, tremor stabilisation and telesurgery.

children.name: Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care
children.blurb: Sepsis, kidney injury, ventilator weaning, falls, and staffing and beds.

children.name: Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation

children.name: Telemedicine and Triage
children.blurb: Symptom routing, camera-based vital signs, wearables, conversational care and mental health signals.

children.name: Epidemiology and Population Health
children.blurb: Syndromic surveillance, outbreak mapping, vaccine waning, social determinants and scarce resource allocation.

children.name: Neuroinformatics and the Brain

children.name: Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security
children.blurb: Enablement audits, local models for patient data, device clearance, bias in triage and connected device security.

sections.body: This field is the practical use of artificial intelligence inside medicine, not a future promise. Right now AI systems read scans, flag possible findings, draft clinical notes from conversations, help plan radiation or surgical paths, watch vital signs in intensive care, screen chemical libraries for drug candidates, answer patient messages in triage, model disease spread, map brain signals, and check whether medical software meets safety rules. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models across these uses, along with 732 AI tools. The work is narrow and task specific, a model that finds a lung nodule on a chest image is not the same model that predicts sepsis in an ICU.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The honest position is uneven. Some areas, like imaging and certain documentation tasks, have cleared regulatory hurdles and are used daily in hospitals, while others, like genomic treatment matching or brain decoding, remain mostly research. The site records 805 scientific models, which shows how much of this work is still being validated rather than deployed. Six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies are tracked, a reminder that real failures carry real harm. Limits include models that perform well on one hospital's data but degrade elsewhere, systems that explain themselves poorly, and a regulatory apparatus still catching up to software that changes after approval.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader wanting to see where AI is most established should start with Diagnostic Imaging and Radiology, then compare it with Genomic Medicine and Precision Therapeutics, where the gap between promise and bedside use is wider. Clinical Documentation and Ambient Intelligence and Telemedicine and Triage cover the parts patients and clinicians touch most directly, while Surgical Robotics and Navigation and Predictive Patient Analytics and Intensive Care show AI acting in high stakes physical and time sensitive settings. Drug Discovery and Molecular Simulation and Epidemiology and Population Health move from the individual body to molecules and whole populations. Neuroinformatics and the Brain is the least settled of the ten, and Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security is the page to read after the others, because it explains the rules, audits, and security failures that constrain all of them. The 210 compliance and regulation pages and 686 glossary terms support that final page and the section as a whole.
